subtopic_detail: Toddler iron deficiency anaemia oral iron
stem:
A 22-month-old girl presents to your general practice for a routine check because her mother is worried she is pale and less energetic than her older sibling was at the same age. She was born at term with an uncomplicated pregnancy and was breastfed until 11 months when she moved to cow's milk. She currently drinks around 900 mL of cow's milk daily from a bottle and eats a mostly beige diet of pasta, bread and biscuits.

On examination she is alert and interactive; conjunctival pallor is noted and there is no jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Growth is on the 25th centile for weight and 50th for height, tracking her prior curve. She has no bruising. Her father is of Anglo-Australian background; her mother is of Italian background with no history of anaemia. Recent bloods show haemoglobin 88 g/L (105-135), mean cell volume 62 fL (75-87), mean cell haemoglobin 21 pg (25-33), reticulocytes 0.4 percent, ferritin 6 mcg/L (30-300) and transferrin saturation 6 percent. Haemoglobin electrophoresis is normal for age.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, conjunctival pallor, no jaundice, no organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Hb 88 g/L (105-135); MCV 62 fL (75-87); MCH 21 pg (25-33); reticulocytes 0.4 percent; ferritin 6 mcg/L (30-300); transferrin saturation 6 percent; haemoglobin electrophoresis normal for age; coeliac screen pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Refer for packed red cell transfusion because the haemoglobin is below 90 g/L in a symptomatic toddler
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for symptomatic anaemia with cardiovascular compromise; oral iron plus dietary change is standard for iron deficiency at this haemoglobin. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Start oral iron 3 mg per kilogram per day of elemental iron and cap cow's milk intake at 500 mL daily
options.rationale: RCH treatment for iron deficiency is 3-6 mg/kg/day elemental iron with dietary iron optimisation; excess cow's milk suppresses iron absorption and appetite. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Arrange intravenous iron polymaltose infusion under paediatric day-stay supervision this week
options.rationale: IV iron is reserved for failed oral iron, malabsorption or intolerance; first-line is oral iron with dietary optimisation. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Trial a strictly gluten-free diet for eight weeks and repeat the full blood count without iron therapy
options.rationale: A gluten-free diet without a coeliac diagnosis is not indicated and delays proven iron replacement; coeliac serology is being investigated but does not delay iron. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Give a single intramuscular iron dextran injection today and review in 6 weeks with a repeat full blood count
options.rationale: Intramuscular iron is painful and rarely used in children; parenteral iron is intravenous where indicated. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

explanation.summary: Toddler iron deficiency is common in children on high cow's milk intake and low iron-rich solids. Diagnosis is a low ferritin (below 12-15 mcg/L in children) with microcytic hypochromic anaemia. Treatment is oral iron 3-6 mg/kg/day of elemental iron, best taken with vitamin C-containing juice and away from milk. Cap cow's milk at 500 mL/day and encourage haem sources and iron-fortified cereals, continuing iron for at least 3 months after normalisation. Investigate for coeliac disease if history suggests malabsorption or if response is poor.
key_points: Oral elemental iron 3-6 mg/kg/day is first-line.
Cap cow's milk at 500 mL/day and encourage iron-rich solids.
Continue iron for 3 months after haemoglobin normalises.
IV iron is reserved for failed oral therapy or malabsorption.
explanation.pearls: Toddlers on more than 600 mL cow's milk per day are at high risk of iron deficiency; treat with elemental iron 3-6 mg/kg/day and cap milk at 500 mL daily.

subtopic_detail: Constipation with red flags requiring investigation
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-week-old boy in outpatients referred by his GP for infrequent stools since birth. He passed his first meconium at 52 hours after birth requiring digital stimulation, and he now opens his bowels every 4 to 7 days with small hard pellets that only pass after a rectal thermometer. He is exclusively breastfed on demand. His weight has dropped from the 50th to the 10th centile since birth.

On examination his abdomen is visibly distended with palpable stool in the left iliac fossa. Rectal examination by the consultant reveals a tight anal sphincter with an empty rectum, followed by an explosive release of foul-smelling stool and gas as the finger is withdrawn. Perianal skin is intact with no fissures visible. There is no lower limb weakness and the anocutaneous reflex is present. He has never had bloody stools. Antenatal and perinatal courses were uneventful.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148/min, blood pressure 78/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 42/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Distended abdomen, palpable left iliac fossa stool, tight anal tone, empty rectum with explosive release on withdrawal of examining finger
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits; urea and electrolytes within normal limits; thyroid function tests pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Trial two weeks of oral macrogol 3350 with review before considering any further investigation
options.rationale: Trial of laxative is appropriate for functional constipation but not for a neonate with delayed meconium, explosive stool on withdrawal and faltering growth. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Request abdominal ultrasound to assess for anatomical obstruction and mesenteric adenopathy
options.rationale: Ultrasound has low yield for Hirschsprung disease and does not visualise the aganglionic segment reliably. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery for suction rectal biopsy to investigate for Hirschsprung disease
options.rationale: Delayed meconium beyond 48 hours, explosive stool on rectal examination and faltering growth in a neonate are red flags for Hirschsprung disease; suction rectal biopsy is the diagnostic gold standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Order abdominal radiograph and start daily glycerol suppositories while awaiting the film report
options.rationale: Radiography adds little in Hirschsprung workup and glycerol suppositories treat symptoms without diagnosing the underlying aganglionosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Send stool for calprotectin and reducing substances to exclude inflammatory bowel disease
options.rationale: Inflammatory bowel disease is exceptionally rare in neonates and the clinical picture points to Hirschsprung, not inflammatory disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Neonatal constipation red flags mandate a search for organic cause. Hirschsprung disease presents with delayed meconium passage beyond 48 hours after birth, chronic distension, poor growth and the classic tight anal tone with an empty rectum plus explosive stool release on withdrawal of the examining finger. Diagnostic workup includes abdominal radiograph showing distal obstruction and contrast enema showing a transition zone; suction rectal biopsy is the gold standard, demonstrating absent ganglion cells and hypertrophied nerve trunks. Definitive treatment is surgical pull-through. Functional constipation and cow's milk protein allergy are more common in infants but do not typically cause delayed meconium.
key_points: Delayed meconium past 48 hours is a red flag for Hirschsprung disease.
Explosive stool on rectal exam withdrawal is a classic sign.
Suction rectal biopsy is the gold standard investigation.
Definitive management is surgical pull-through.
explanation.pearls: In a neonate with delayed meconium beyond 48 hours, tight anal tone and explosive release on rectal exam, refer for suction rectal biopsy for Hirschsprung disease rather than trialling laxatives.

stem:
You are the GP shared-care doctor reviewing a 34-year-old woman at 27 weeks gestation with her first pregnancy. She has no personal history of diabetes but her mother has type 2 diabetes managed on metformin. Her booking BMI was 29 kg/m2. She has had no antenatal complications so far and foetal movements are normal.

Her 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 26 weeks reports fasting plasma glucose 5.4 mmol/L, 1 hour plasma glucose 9.6 mmol/L and 2 hour plasma glucose 8.3 mmol/L. She is asymptomatic. Foetal biometry today shows growth appropriate for gestation with an abdominal circumference on the 60th centile.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Symphyseal-fundal height 27 cm, foetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Investigations: OGTT fasting 5.4 mmol/L (<5.1); 1 hour 9.6 mmol/L (<10.0); 2 hour 8.3 mmol/L (<8.5); HbA1c 5.6 percent

lead_in: Which of the following best describes the interpretation and next management step?

options.text: Normal OGTT; continue routine antenatal care and repeat OGTT only if polyhydramnios or macrosomia develops later
options.rationale: Fasting 5.4 mmol/L exceeds the ADIPS diagnostic threshold of 5.1 mmol/L so this is diagnostic of GDM. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guideline for the Testing and Diagnosis of GDM)
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guideline for the Testing and Diagnosis of GDM

options.text: Impaired glucose tolerance; repeat OGTT at 32 weeks and defer any dietary intervention until that repeat test
options.rationale: ADIPS uses single-threshold criteria on any of the three values; there is no intermediate impaired glucose tolerance category diagnosed antenatally. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guideline for the Testing and Diagnosis of GDM)
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guideline for the Testing and Diagnosis of GDM

options.text: Overt diabetes in pregnancy; start immediate insulin therapy without a trial of lifestyle and dietary modification
options.rationale: Overt diabetes in pregnancy requires fasting 7.0 or higher, random 11.1 or higher, HbA1c 6.5 percent or higher; none apply so this is GDM, not overt diabetes. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guideline for the Testing and Diagnosis of GDM)
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guideline for the Testing and Diagnosis of GDM

options.text: GDM; refer to a diabetes-in-pregnancy service, start diet and lifestyle change and begin glucose self-monitoring
options.rationale: Fasting 5.4 mmol/L exceeds the ADIPS threshold; management is multidisciplinary with diet and exercise, self-monitoring and metformin or insulin if targets not met. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guideline for the Testing and Diagnosis of GDM)
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guideline for the Testing and Diagnosis of GDM

options.text: GDM; commence metformin 500 mg twice daily immediately as first-line without an initial dietary trial period
options.rationale: Initial management of GDM is a dietary and exercise trial with self-monitoring; pharmacotherapy begins if targets not achieved after 1 to 2 weeks. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guideline for the Testing and Diagnosis of GDM)
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guideline for the Testing and Diagnosis of GDM

explanation.summary: The ADIPS 75 g OGTT diagnostic thresholds for GDM at 24-28 weeks are fasting 5.1 mmol/L or higher, 1 hour 10.0 mmol/L or higher, or 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L or higher. Any single value meets diagnosis. Overt diabetes in pregnancy is defined by fasting 7.0 mmol/L or higher, random 11.1 mmol/L or higher, or HbA1c 6.5 percent or higher and requires immediate specialist input. GDM initial management is lifestyle modification plus 1-2 week trial with self-monitoring targets fasting under 5.0 mmol/L and 2-hour postprandial under 6.7 mmol/L. If targets not met, metformin or insulin is added; insulin remains the mainstay for tight fasting control.
key_points: ADIPS fasting threshold for GDM is 5.1 mmol/L; 1 hr 10.0; 2 hr 8.5.
Any single value exceeding threshold diagnoses GDM.
First-line is diet, exercise and self-monitoring for 1-2 weeks.
Add metformin or insulin if targets not met.
explanation.pearls: ADIPS GDM thresholds on 75 g OGTT: fasting 5.1, 1 hour 10.0, 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L; any one value at threshold diagnoses GDM.

sources.label: ADIPS Consensus Guideline for the Testing and Diagnosis of GDM

subtopic_detail: Group B streptococcus intrapartum prophylaxis indication
stem:
You are the birth suite registrar. A 29-year-old G2P1 woman at 39 weeks gestation is admitted in early labour. Her routine 36-week vaginal-rectal swab was negative for group B streptococcus. Her previous baby was born at term by normal vaginal delivery in Sydney and required intravenous benzylpenicillin at 12 hours old for a positive blood culture that grew Streptococcus agalactiae. She has no penicillin allergy.

On arrival contractions are every 5 minutes, cervix is 4 cm dilated and the membranes have just ruptured spontaneously with clear liquor. She is well; foetal heart rate on intermittent auscultation is reassuring. She has no fever, no known urinary GBS bacteriuria this pregnancy and no antenatal complications.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 90/min, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm dilated 50 percent effaced, cephalic presentation, clear liquor draining, foetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Investigations: 36-week vaginal-rectal GBS swab negative; urine culture this pregnancy no growth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis?

options.text: Withhold antibiotics because the current pregnancy swab is negative and rely on paediatric observation of the newborn
options.rationale: A previous infant with invasive GBS disease is a standalone indication for prophylaxis in every subsequent pregnancy regardless of current swab. (Source: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus in Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus in Pregnancy

options.text: Give intravenous cefazolin 2 g and repeat 1 g every 8 hours because non-anaphylactic penicillin allergy is possible
options.rationale: There is no penicillin allergy history; benzylpenicillin is preferred first-line. (Source: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus in Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus in Pregnancy

options.text: Give oral amoxicillin 1 g stat and continue three times daily for the remainder of labour without intravenous therapy
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics do not achieve adequate foetal tissue concentrations rapidly enough; intravenous therapy is standard. (Source: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus in Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus in Pregnancy

options.text: Repeat the vaginal-rectal swab now and only start antibiotics if positive result returns before delivery
options.rationale: Swab result would not return in time and prior invasive GBS disease already mandates prophylaxis in this pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus in Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus in Pregnancy

options.text: Give intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading dose then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery for GBS prophylaxis
options.rationale: Previous infant with invasive GBS disease is a standalone RANZCOG indication regardless of current swab; benzylpenicillin is first-line. (Source: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus in Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus in Pregnancy

explanation.summary: RANZCOG intrapartum GBS prophylaxis is indicated in any of: positive maternal GBS colonisation in current pregnancy, prior infant with invasive GBS disease, GBS bacteriuria this pregnancy at any count, unknown GBS status with intrapartum fever, prolonged rupture of membranes (18 hours or more) or preterm labour under 37 weeks. First-line is intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading dose then 1.8 g every 4 hours. Cefazolin is used for non-anaphylactic penicillin allergy; clindamycin (if susceptible) or vancomycin for anaphylactic allergy. Adequate coverage is defined as at least one dose 4 or more hours before delivery.
key_points: Prior invasive GBS infant mandates prophylaxis regardless of current swab.
IV benzylpenicillin is first-line; 3 g load then 1.8 g every 4 hours.
Cefazolin for non-anaphylactic allergy; vancomycin for anaphylactic.
Adequate cover is at least one dose 4 or more hours before delivery.
explanation.pearls: In labour, a previous infant with invasive GBS disease alone is a standalone indication for intravenous benzylpenicillin prophylaxis even if the current pregnancy swab is negative.

sources.label: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus in Pregnancy
Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis

stem:
You are the on-call registrar. A 31-year-old woman with severe pre-eclampsia has just had a spontaneous vaginal delivery at 38 weeks. She had labetalol running throughout and her most recent blood pressure was 158/102 mmHg. Placenta was delivered spontaneously and appears complete on inspection. Estimated blood loss so far is 1200 mL and continues to flow briskly.

On examination the fundus is boggy but there is no obvious trauma. Bimanual compression is initiated by your midwifery colleague and intravenous access is confirmed patent. Uterine massage produces a small transient contraction. Bloods are being sent. The patient is alert and speaking but pale. IV oxytocin 10 units has been given as part of active management and a further 40 units infusion in 1 litre normal saline is running.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 158/102 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Boggy uterus, no visible tear on speculum, moderate ongoing dark blood loss, bimanual compression in progress
data_table.Investigations: Estimated blood loss 1200 mL and continuing; Hb pending; group and hold sent; coagulation panel pending

lead_in: Which uterotonic is the most appropriate next agent given her clinical picture?

options.text: Carboprost 250 microgram intramuscular repeated every 15 minutes to a maximum of 8 doses
options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertensive women; carboprost is the appropriate escalation when oxytocin is already running and hypertension precludes ergometrine. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Ergometrine 250 microgram intramuscular repeat once as second-line agent after ongoing oxytocin infusion
options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia because it precipitates hypertensive crisis. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Syntometrine 1 mL intramuscular containing 5 units oxytocin and 500 microgram ergometrine combined
options.rationale: Syntometrine contains ergometrine and is contraindicated in hypertension for the same reason. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Misoprostol 800 microgram sublingual and re-dose at 60 minutes if bleeding persists
options.rationale: Misoprostol is an option in resource-poor settings; in Australian tertiary units carboprost is preferred second-line for atony refractory to oxytocin. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous as monotherapy in place of additional uterotonic agents
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid is a valuable adjunct to uterotonics but does not replace an additional uterotonic when uterine atony continues. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: Primary postpartum haemorrhage is blood loss of 500 mL or more within 24 hours of vaginal birth (1000 mL for caesarean), most commonly from uterine atony. Management combines bimanual compression and bladder emptying, uterotonic escalation, tranexamic acid within 3 hours of onset, and blood product resuscitation. Ergometrine and syntometrine are contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia because they trigger hypertensive crisis, so the escalation ladder skips to carboprost intramuscularly. Misoprostol is used where carboprost is unavailable, and refractory bleeding leads to balloon tamponade, uterine artery embolisation or surgery.
key_points: Ergometrine and syntometrine are contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia.
Carboprost is the appropriate second-line agent after oxytocin in these patients.
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV should be given within 3 hours of onset as adjunct.
Consider balloon tamponade or surgery for refractory bleeding.
explanation.pearls: In postpartum haemorrhage with hypertension or pre-eclampsia, skip ergometrine and syntometrine and escalate directly from oxytocin to carboprost 250 microgram intramuscular.

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar receiving a 28-year-old G1P0 woman at 30+2 weeks gestation from a rural transfer with regular painful contractions for 4 hours. Speculum shows cervix 3 cm dilated with intact membranes. Foetal fibronectin was positive on the referring hospital assessment. She has no vaginal bleeding, no fever and no history of asthma. Booking blood pressure was 108/68 mmHg and today's is 118/72 mmHg. Foetal heart rate on continuous cardiotocography is reassuring with baseline 145/min and normal variability.

She has already received the first dose of intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg. Neonatal intensive care is available on site. Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection is being prepared. She has no drug allergies and no significant past medical history.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Regular contractions every 3 minutes; cervix 3 cm dilated 60 percent effaced; membranes intact; cephalic presentation
data_table.Investigations: Foetal fibronectin positive; foetal cardiotocography baseline 145/min normal variability; full blood count within normal limits; urea and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: Which tocolytic is the most appropriate first-line choice to buy time for corticosteroid completion and transfer?

options.text: Salbutamol 100 microgram intravenous infusion titrated to slow contractions over the next 12 hours
options.rationale: Beta agonists cause significant maternal cardiovascular side effects and are no longer preferred first-line in Australian practice. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour Statement)

options.text: Nifedipine 20 mg oral immediate release stat, then 20 mg every 30 minutes for two further doses if contractions persist
options.rationale: Nifedipine is the first-line tocolytic in Australian practice with a favourable maternal safety profile and equivalent efficacy to atosiban. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour Statement)

options.text: Atosiban 6.75 mg intravenous bolus then 300 microgram per minute infusion for 3 hours as first-line agent
options.rationale: Atosiban is effective but is not typically first-line in Australia due to cost; nifedipine is preferred initial choice. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour Statement)

options.text: Indomethacin 100 mg per rectum then 25 mg every 6 hours for 48 hours as tocolysis regardless of the gestation involved
options.rationale: Indomethacin is used only under 32 weeks for limited duration due to premature ductus arteriosus closure risk; nifedipine is broader-use first-line. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour Statement)

options.text: Magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenous loading dose then 1 g per hour as combined tocolysis and neuroprotection
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is used for neuroprotection under 30 weeks but is not effective as a tocolytic; a separate tocolytic is required. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour Statement)

explanation.summary: The aim of tocolysis in preterm labour is to delay delivery by 48 hours so antenatal corticosteroids can act and in-utero transfer can occur if required. Nifedipine is the Australian first-line agent based on efficacy equivalent to atosiban, oral administration, low cost and acceptable side-effect profile. Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular is given as two doses 24 hours apart when delivery is anticipated between 24 and 34+6 weeks. Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection is used at gestations under 30 weeks; indomethacin is reserved for gestations under 32 weeks for up to 48 hours.
key_points: Nifedipine is the Australian first-line tocolytic in preterm labour.
Aim is 48 hours delay for antenatal steroid effect and transfer.
Magnesium sulfate is neuroprotective, not tocolytic, and used under 30 weeks.
Indomethacin only under 32 weeks and limited to 48 hours.
explanation.pearls: For preterm labour under 34 weeks in Australia, first-line tocolysis is nifedipine 20 mg oral stat then titrated dosing to buy 48 hours for corticosteroid effect.
